items.title: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain
items.summary: Every year around the Hindu festival of Diwali, or Deepavali, residents in Nepal observe Kaag Tihar, an annual festival day dedicated to worshipping house crows as divine messengers. However, in the country’s capital, rapid urban sprawl, habitat degradation and changing perceptions toward the bird are testing human-crow relations, reports Mongabay’s Gobinda Pokharel. Satellite analysis shows Kathmandu’s urban build-up area expanded by 124% between 1989 and 2018, while another study found municipal green space plummeted by 54% between 1975 and 2025. Meanwhile, the removal of more than 2,000 mature trees along major thoroughfares like the Kathmandu Ring Road has forced house crows (Corvus splendens) to nest on utility poles and electrical wires, according to a 2024 study led by Tribhuvan University researcher Dinesh Bhusal, in Nepal. “When old and large trees are cut down, specialist birds lose their habitats,” said Hem Bahadur Katuwal, a bird ecologist at the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, southwest China. “Eventually, only functional generalist species, such as crows, which can survive under almost any conditions, remain.” Compounding the population shift is Kathmandu’s unmanaged refuse. Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and uncovered trash at meat shops provide abundant forage, attracting dense concentrations of crows and black kites (Milvus migrans). “Large quantities of discarded food and exposed waste from meat shops have contributed to the unusual increase in crows and kites in Kathmandu,” said Kamal Raj Gosai, an…
items.t: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain

items.title: The long reach of El Niño impacts on Southeast Asia’s primates
items.summary: As Indonesia’s El-Niño driven fires spark a race to save endangered orangutans and other wildlife, a recent review paper, published in the journal Oryx, is raising concerns about both the short- and long-term impacts on primates of such climatic events in Southeast Asia. “Primates might survive a fire, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us whether they’re going to have enough food or suitable habitat, or what’s happening with their health and ability to reproduce in the months and years ahead,” said Elizabeth Barrow, lead author of the paper and conservation research director at the Gunung Palung Orangutan Conservation Program (GPOCP), Indonesia. With 94% of Southeast Asia’s primates threatened with extinction, the impact of El Niño is a poorly understood but significant threat to populations, according to the researchers. “From my perspective, this is a huge conservation issue for primates in Southeast Asia,” Barrow said. Habitat loss and degradation caused by drought and fire are linked to several concerning impacts. They can drive changes in diet, behavior and the physical condition of primates, the review found. Primate populations can become crowded as forest areas shrink, while others may be displaced, suffer localized extirpations, or increased infant mortality. In total, however, the review identified only 15 papers on the impacts of El Niño-linked drought, fire and smoke on primates. Research was limited to just seven of 105 primate species, and entirely focused on Indonesia, leaving major knowledge gaps. “Although there are very few papers, the effects on primates…
items.t: The long reach of El Niño impacts on Southeast Asia’s primates

items.title: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera
items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — On a rainy Saturday morning, 57-year-old fisher Sheriff Kamara sat among other community members inside a wooden makeshift shelter in Sierra Leone’s Mahera Beach, waiting for the weather to improve. Along the shoreline, discarded plastic bottles, water sachets, bags and food wrappers lay scattered among old footwear and foam. For Kamara, plastic waste has become a regular problem, increasingly affecting his ability to fish and earn a living. “When I started fishing, it was rare to find anything in my net besides fish. But now, it is a weekly, sometimes a daily, problem,” he tells Mongabay. According to Kamara, a lot of single-use plastic waste frequently gets caught in his fishing nets, particularly near the shore after a heavy rain. Removing the entangled plastic waste takes considerable time and effort. “I find all sorts of plastic in my net almost every week. Removing the plastics with my apprentice’s help takes a lot of time,” he says. For fishermen like him, plastic pollution is not just an environmental concern but an additional burden on their daily work and livelihoods. To support the fishing communities, the government launched a fisheries and marine resources strategy in 2025, which provides a 10-year framework for promoting sustainable fisheries management, protecting marine ecosystems and improving livelihoods. It also calls for sustainable use of marine resources and stronger protection for the fisheries sector. Plastic waste, including discarded bottles and containers, accumulated along the shoreline beneath fishing boats. Image by…
items.t: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera

items.title: Peruvian officials reportedly increase tally to more than 12,000 tarantulas in recent seizure
items.summary: Peruvian authorities have updated the number of tarantulas seized in a recent wildlife trafficking case from 3,000 to more than 12,000, according to South American media reports. The final count of 12,796 seized spiders was reportedly announced by the Peruvian National Police (PNP). The authorities said they believe these arachnids are worth more than half a million euros (around $548,000) on the international market. On Nov. 4, 2026, the Peruvian National Forest and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) announced it seized thousands of tarantulas at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima, hidden inside socks and plastic containers in luggage destined for Germany. Authorities arrested two German citizens and a Polish national, including a “renowned tarantula researcher” who was not publicly identified, and detained them for further investigation at the time. The seized tarantulas included individuals in different life stages, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, and came from across Peru. They included blue bird eaters (Thrixopelma lagunas), Bolivian blue leg bird eater (Pamphobeteus antinous), members of the genus Pamphobeteus  and several newly described species. Authorities said the alleged traffickers collected the spiders from the wild to sell as exotic pets to collectors and for research. None of the seized species are internationally protected under CITES, the global wildlife treaty. However, they are protected nationally under Peruvian laws, and removing them from the wild is an offense. In a TV program, General José Manuel Cruz Chamba from the PNP reportedly identified one…
items.t: Peruvian officials reportedly increase tally to more than 12,000 tarantulas in recent seizure

items.title: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
items.summary: The International Energy Agency reports that the energy shock from the Iran war is reshaping global energy strategies. Released Thursday, the report highlights how countries are prioritizing energy security and affordability, benefiting renewable technologies like solar and nuclear power. The IEA warns that the crisis’s effects will deepen the longer it lasts. At the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, electrification and reducing fossil fuel reliance are key issues. The IEA projects a decrease in oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz and an increase in solar and nuclear power. Energy demand for cooling has overtaken heating for the first time this year. By Anton L. Delgado and Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Banner image: People walk near solar panels at a photovoltaic power station operated by Huadian (Beijing) New Energy Development Co. Ltd. in Beijing, Sept. 23, 2026. Image courtesy of Achmad Ibrahim, Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says

items.title: In Sri Lanka, human actions are driving wild animals into cities and suburbs
items.summary: COLOMBO – It was a surprise for Mohamed Fareed, a resident of Jawatte, an upscale neighborhood in Sri Lanka’s commercial capital Colombo, to find a peacock near his house back in 2020. Today, there are at least 12 peacocks, including peahens roaming the area. “In the mornings and evenings, we hear their loud and piercing calls and now the neighborhood is used to their presence,” he told Mongabay. “Sometimes we see them on rooftops. Children are quite excited to see them. These peacocks frequent the area near the mosque to feed on pigeon feed inside the Jawatte mosque.” Peacocks have been frequently spotted in densely populated areas such as Kollupitiya and Mount Lavinia and, similar to Fareed, many residents are seeing peacocks near their home for the first time in their lives, and the numbers are increasing. items.t: In Sri Lanka, human actions are driving wild animals into cities and suburbs

items.title: “Rooting For Her”: Cincinnati Zoo Updates Public On Fiona The Hippo After She Swallowed A Child’s Knitted Hat
items.summary:
A child’s visit to Cincinnati Zoo on November 8 took an alarming turn for one of the habitat’s best-known residents, leaving her in need of round-the-clock supervision. 

Fiona , the beloved nine-year-old hippo whose premature birth and remarkable survival captured hearts around the world in 2017, swallowed a knitted item thrown into her enclosure by the young guest. 

What initially appeared to be something the animal might overcome without difficulty has since developed into a more concerning situation, with her appetite beginning to decline and raising concerns among her veterinary team. 

As specialists explore ways to help Fiona pass the object naturally, her caregivers have turned to an unconventional piece of equipment in the hope of aiding her recovery. 

Zookeepers try an unusual recovery method as beloved hippo remains under close veterinary watch 

cincinnatizoo/Instagram 

According to zoo spokeswoman Michelle Curley, a kid’s knitted hat became caught in a ceiling fan as they tossed it before being propelled through a small opening above the viewing windows and into Fiona’s enclosure. 

Fiona swallowed the item, although she did not initially show any signs of discomfort. 

In a video update shared by the zoo on November 17, a member of the veterinary staff explained that they had expected the relatively small object to pass through her digestive system. 

However, that did not happen as anticipated. 

cincinnatizoo/Instagram 

After the hat remained in her stomach for several days, Fiona began eating less, triggering further…

items.title: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe
items.summary: LONDON — On Nov. 10, Mongabay went to the site of the annual meeting of the body that regulates fishing in the northeastern Atlantic, where a little-known geopolitical dispute over marine resources was playing out behind closed doors. The North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC), a multilateral body, governs the fishing of three major stocks of fish in international waters near Europe, as well as associated species and habitats. Disagreement between countries over how to manage the stocks has had serious consequences, experts say. All three species — Atlantic mackerel (Scomber scombrus), Atlanto-Scandian herring (Clupea harengus), and blue whiting (Micromesistius poutassou) — have been subject to overfishing for years. The Northeast Atlantic mackerel population is in particularly bad shape, currently 22% below the NEAFC’s target threshold, having been fished above scientifically advised levels every year since 2008. The NEAFC is one of the world’s 17 regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), and a fisheries governance campaigner has called it the most “fraught” and “problematic.” It has six member parties: the European Union, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Norway, Russia, and Denmark (on behalf of the Faroe Islands and Greenland; the delegation is commonly called DFG). The three fish species are prey for marine mammals and seabirds, and are sought after on global markets. Mackerel is sold in tins, herring is eaten pickled or smoked, and blue whiting is used for aquaculture feed. At this year’s annual meeting, held Nov. 10-13 in London, the parties made no…
items.t: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe

items.title: 44 Astonishing Photos Of The Animal Kingdom’s Hunters, Shared By Wildlife Photographers
items.summary:
In the wild, a single photograph can tell a story of patience, instinct, and survival. A tiny spider carrying its catch, an eagle gripping its meal high above the ground, or a big cat standing proudly beside its latest hunt - these are fleeting scenes that reveal a side of the animal kingdom we don't often get to witness up close. And while nature is full of beautiful sights, some of its most compelling moments are far less predictable. 

For wildlife photographers, getting a shot like this is no small feat. Animals rarely follow a script, and the most interesting encounters can unfold in seconds. It takes a keen eye, plenty of patience, and a little luck to capture these interactions before they disappear into the wilderness. 

Recently, a Threads post invited wildlife photographers to share their best photographs of animals with their prey. The thread brought together an array of remarkable images, offering glimpses of different species in the middle of their natural routines.

items.title: Central-north Amazonia has experienced an ‘alarming’ increase in temperatures: Study
items.summary: A small team of scientists was counting plants for a forest census near Manaus in northern Brazil when fire season started in October 2023. Some days the smoke was too thick to see; on other days it was too hot to wear conventional masks, so Aretha Guimarães, a biologist with Brazil’s National Institute of Amazonian Research (INPA) and her colleagues covered their faces with wet bandages in order to breathe. Even through the bandages and smoke, the smell of dead, rotting sloths was overpowering, Guimarães remembers. “Animals just kept showing up dead,” she told Mongabay over a video call. “I’ve never seen such mortality. We were shocked.” Over the following months, Guimarães and her team found dead sloths in every part of the forest they studied; some still hanging from branches. Most, they assumed, could not move quickly enough to find water when temperatures started to rise. “I can’t explain what happened, because I’ve never seen such a thing.” For decades, research has highlighted southern Amazonia, thousands of kilometers away, as the region’s climate change hotspot, where average temperatures are increasing faster than the north, exacerbated by deforestation and sweeping forest fires. Recent research published in September in Nature, however, identifies the central-north part of the Amazon Basin as the vanguard of an “alarming” increase in temperatures and dry conditions. Analyzing satellite, aircraft and observation station data between 1981-2023, the researchers found that across all of Amazonia, extreme temperatures increased more than twice as quickly as annual…
items.t: Central-north Amazonia has experienced an ‘alarming’ increase in temperatures: Study

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
items.t: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

items.title: Threatened species make up half of shark catches at Indonesian fishing port, study finds
items.summary: JAKARTA — In Muncar, a busy fishing port on the southeastern coast of Indonesia’s East Java province, sharks can fetch as much as 1.5 million rupiah each, or about $82. However, their value to fishing communities comes at a cost to conservation: Threatened species, including the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), made up a substantial share of the sharks landed at Muncar. A study published earlier this year in the journal Oryx examined shark catches landed in Muncar between 2023 and 2024. Researchers combined catch records with interviews with fishers, landing data, and GPS data to investigate which species were caught, where fishing took place, and which practices posed the greatest risks to threatened species. The findings revealed a worrying pattern. According to the study, 50% of recorded shark catches comprised species classified as threatened on the Red List of the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority. A third of species were listed on CITES, which regulates the global trade in protected wildlife. Scalloped hammerheads accounted for 11.7% of recorded catches. Other frequently caught species included the silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis), spinner shark (Carcharhinus brevipinna), and blacktip reef shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus), all listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List; and the pelagic thresher shark (Alopias pelagicus), listed as endangered. All five species appear in CITES Appendix II, which means their international trade is highly restricted. In an interview with Mongabay, corresponding author Osmaleli, a lecturer…
items.t: Threatened species make up half of shark catches at Indonesian fishing port, study finds

items.title: Skinks in boots: How Hong Kong emerges as key hub in Australia’s native reptile trafficking
items.summary: HONG KONG — Two days after Christmas last year, customs authorities at Hong Kong International Airport intercepted a consignment from Australia and found 13 live lizards bound and stuffed inside sheepskin winter shoes, popularly known as ugg boots. The air cargo was falsely declared to contain snacks, Hong Kong’s Customs said in a press release in late December 2025. But instead, inside were assorted lizard species, including the shingleback skink (Tiliqua rugosa). Between March 2025 and July 2026, Customs announced at least three other seizures of live reptiles found in consignments from Australia. In the four cases, customs officers confiscated 98 live animals — 74 lizards and 24 snakes — with the total value exceeding 1.1 million Hong Kong dollars ($141,100). All but one lizard were believed to be listed in the global wildlife trade convention CITES appendices. According to Hong Kong authorities, most of these seizures are under investigation, and one was dropped. No arrests have been made. Despite Australia’s comprehensive ban on commercial exports of live native species since 1982, the rarity and unique looks of its reptiles have made them coveted in pet markets around the world. And Hong Kong, a major entrepôt in the Asia-Pacific region, has an outsized role in the illegal trade of Australian reptiles. “Hong Kong is a major trafficking hub or destination for Australian reptiles,” said Sam Inglis, wildlife program manager at ADM Capital Foundation (ADMCF), a Hong Kong-based environmental nonprofit that tracks wildlife crime. One of the 13 seized live Australian…
items.t: Skinks in boots: How Hong Kong emerges as key hub in Australia’s native reptile trafficking

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
items.t: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

items.title: World Anteater Day: Rewilding and restoration offer hope for enigmatic species
items.summary: World Anteater Day falls on Nov. 19, in recognition of the tube-nosed, ant- and termite-eating animals living across Central and South America. Closely related to sloths, anteaters generally live in trees. The largest species, the giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), lives on the ground, though, where it rips open anthills and termite nests with its razor-sharp claws and slurps up the insects with its long, sticky tongue. The species is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Giant anteaters have disappeared from parts of their range due to habitat destruction and hunting, but habitat restoration and rewilding efforts are helping their return in some of their former range. A giant anteater’s return in Argentina offers a case for letting nature restore itself In 2025, a giant anteater returned to the Alma Guaraní reserve in Argentina’s Gran Chaco region for the first known time since 1986, reported Mongabay contributor Sean Mowbray. Habitat degradation in the Gran Chaco due to agricultural expansion and forest loss had reduced ant abundance by 30-50% compared to well-preserved areas, directly affecting the giant anteater. Alma Guaraní Natural Reserve, which covers approximately 6,400 hectares (about 15,800 acres), has been the site of volunteer-led restoration work for more than a decade. In some areas, volunteers actively planted native trees; in others, they used fences to allow the land to regenerate naturally, free from incursions by livestock, dogs, and hunting and fishing activity. A network of 20 camera traps found that the giant anteater mostly remained in…
items.t: World Anteater Day: Rewilding and restoration offer hope for enigmatic species

items.title: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters
items.summary:
Smaller species such as swallows and skylarks are more likely to stay near breeding grounds rather than migrate

Bonfire Night is over, Christmas is coming, and Britain’s birds are getting ready for the winter. They must survive the extremes of our weather and make it through to next spring to get the chance to breed again.

Birds have very different strategies to prepare for cold weather. Many smaller birds – swallows and swifts, cuckoos and chats, warblers and flycatchers – simply avoid it by migrating: some fly all the way to sub-Saharan Africa, where they enjoy the benefits of a second spring and summer south of the equator. Others, such as blackbirds and robins, stay put. But if they sense that a cold spell is coming, they too will head south, though not as far – most either remain in south-west Britain or cross the Channel to France or Spain.

Continue reading...
items.t: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters

items.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
items.summary:
Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird, with populations that visit Britain spending summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter.

items.title: Borneo Indigenous groups turn land rights victory into warning for future generations
items.summary: Indigenous communities in Malaysian Borneo gathered on Nov. 4 to place a memorial stone in commemoration of their three-year battle with an oil palm plantation that threatened their native customary land rights and also endangered a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Placing the Ba Besanan Memorial Stone in the forest was partly a celebration by the Berawan, Penan, and Tering peoples, but also a warning to current and future generations about the outside interests seeking to make money off their native customary land, one leader said. “I remind the people that we can’t overstate [the victory],” Willie Kajan, an Indigenous Tering member who represents the Berawan and Tering in Mulu, in the state of Sarawak, told Mongabay by phone. “We don’t know their next tactic.” Ukau Lupung, the representative of the Penan community at Bateu Bungan, places a stone on top of the Ba Besanan Memorial Stone as a symbolic gesture to mark its inauguration  on Nov. 4, 2026 in the Mulu area of Malaysia’s Sarawak state. Image courtesy of Keruan. A surprise victory The Berawan, Penan and Tering peoples live both within and around the nearly 53,000-hectare (131,000-acre) Gunung Mulu National Park, and they rely on the land for their livelihoods and cultural preservation. Indigenous residents first detected logging there in 2018, when employees of Malaysian firm Radiant Lagoon Sdn. Bhd. began clearing land for development. The firm held rights to a 4,400-hectare (nearly 11,000-acre) oil palm concession, which also overlapped with Gunung Mulu National Park — declared a UNESCO…This article was…
items.t: Borneo Indigenous groups turn land rights victory into warning for future generations

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.summary: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

items.title: Greenpeace drops ‘Attenboulder’ to deter UK bottom trawlers in a marine protected area
items.summary: Greenpeace activists recently dropped several enormous boulders in the U.K.’s Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area to discourage destructive bottom trawling currently permitted in the area. The nearly 37,000 square kilometer (about 14,000 square miles) MPA is part of the U.K.’s network of marine protected areas, which contribute to its commitment to the global conservation target of protecting 30% of the Earth’s land and sea by 2030. However, the MPA currently allows bottom trawl fishing, a commercial fishing practice in which a large, weighted net is dragged along the seafloor and scoops up marine life in its path. Greenpeace U.K.’s head of oceans, Elena Polisano, said the MPA amounts to little more than a paper park — a protected area in name only. “In a way it’s false advertising because the marine life isn’t protected in these areas,” Polisano told Mongabay in a video call. “They kind of bulldoze the seabed taking everything in their path,” Polisano said. Bottom trawling is “pulverizing marine life, stripping the ocean of fish and killing porpoises, sharks, dolphins, seabirds,” she added. To create barriers for bottom trawlers, Greenpeace placed 10 boulders, each about 2 tonnes (4,400 pounds), on the seafloor. One was carved in the likeness of naturalist David Attenborough and dubbed “Attenboulder.” Greenpeace shared coordinates for the boulders with authorities and fishers. Polsano said they won’t necessarily stop bottom trawlers, but they will create new obstacles for their operations. The European Bottom Fisheries Alliance decried Greenpeace’s actions saying…
items.t: Greenpeace drops ‘Attenboulder’ to deter UK bottom trawlers in a marine protected area

items.title: Grand Canyon’s South Rim hotels to reopen as park eases water restrictions
items.summary: GRAND CANYON NATIONAL PARK, Ariz. (AP) — Officials at Grand Canyon National Park announced Wednesday that they are easing water restrictions, meaning hotels on the South Rim will once again be able to accommodate overnight guests. The famous El Tovar Hotel along with several other lodges will reopen Friday now that the park has reached a milestone in restoration of water service following severe flooding earlier this year. Flooding in late August caused three deaths, prompted rescues and damaged key infrastructure, including a water intake pump and a significant stretch of a decades-old pipeline that supplied water for millions of visitors to the South Rim and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. At the time, officials said they were just over a month away from completing a more than $200 million upgrade to the 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline. More flooding in September damaged temporary repairs. Although lodging is reopening, park officials urge visitors to conserve as restoration of the water system continues. “Simple actions, including taking shorter showers, turning off faucets when not in use and avoiding unnecessary water use, help support the park’s water system as operations resume,” the park said in its announcement. Food and beverage services will resume gradually, according to park officials. By Associated Press Banner image: The Grand Canyon. Image courtesy of Amy Martin via National Park Service. This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Grand Canyon’s South Rim hotels to reopen as park eases water restrictions

Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment watchdog says

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the “deeply concerning” decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.

New data shows that wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

items.title: Indigenous communities in Panama fear a second dam as damage from first goes unrepaired
items.summary: Nearly two decades after construction began on the CHAN-75 hydroelectric dam project, Indigenous Ngäbe communities in western Panama continue to face severe environmental, cultural and spiritual impacts, according to a new report by the Indigenous rights organization Cultural Survival. It found that communities still suffer from displacement, pollution, the loss of local fish species, medicinal plants, spiritual practices and other threats to their livelihoods. As communities continue to fight for reparations, Panamanian authorities have granted a concession for a second dam on the same river. Ismael Quintero, a Ngäbe leader of the Guayabal community, said their lives changed completely when the state-owned electric power generation company Empresa de Generación Eléctrica (EGESA) began to build the first dam in 2007. “Crops were abundant, and there was free navigation along the Changuinola River,” he told Mongabay via WhatsApp voice messages. “Our whole family enjoyed the clean and healthy river at that time.” For the Ngäbe people, the river traditionally holds deep spiritual and cultural significance. Quintero said it provides them with food, such as fish and shrimp, and serves as a source of inspiration and strength. It is sacred to them, he added. They traditionally believe that a spirit — the owner of the fish and river ecosystems — resides within it, and therefore, any catch is a gift from this spirit. For this reason, they offer prayers to the spirit before undertaking any activities there. Tilapia fish caught in the Changuinola River by a member of a Ngäbe…
items.t: Indigenous communities in Panama fear a second dam as damage from first goes unrepaired

items.title: 50 Glimpses Of Wildlife Thriving Just Outside People’s Windows, Shared Online
items.summary:
Wildlife photography is usually associated with remote places: savannas, rainforests, frozen tundras, and photographers who travel thousands of miles for a single frame. But some of the most memorable encounters with wild animals don’t require a passport or a long lens. They happen just past the back door, on a fence post, beneath a bird feeder, or at the edge of a lawn as the light starts to fade. 

These moments are easy to miss. A backyard visitor rarely announces itself, and it rarely stays long. It might appear for a few seconds while the coffee is brewing or slip through the garden at dusk when no one is watching. Catching it on camera takes the same things any wildlife photographer relies on: patience, a quiet presence, and the instinct to grab the camera before the moment disappears. 

National Geographic, a name synonymous with extraordinary wildlife photography for more than a century, recently turned its attention closer to home. In a post on Threads, the brand invited its followers to show the wildlife they’ve spotted in their own backyards, and people responded in force. The replies quickly filled with photos of wild neighbors captured from porches, gardens, and windows, each one a reminder that nature doesn’t stop at the city limits or the property line. 

Below are 50 of the best photos people shared under National Geographic’s post; take a look.  

More info: threads.com

items.title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
items.summary:
Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry

A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.

DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

items.title: Study maps jaguars across the Americas to help their populations rebound
items.summary: Residents of a neighborhood in Foz do Iguaçu, in southern Brazil, alerted authorities after spotting a jaguar (Panthera onca) roaming the streets in June 2026. One family was even more surprised when, one morning, they heard a loud commotion and found the animal on their porch. Following a major mobilization involving police, environmental agencies and organizations specializing in the species, the male jaguar was sedated and temporarily taken to a wildlife refuge. A few weeks later, the animal, named Tape’ỹ — a word meaning “the one who lost his way” in the Indigenous Tupi-Guarani language — was released into Iguaçu National Park, near where he had been found. “Jaguars need large areas of habitat to survive. And it’s not enough for these areas to exist: They must be connected, allowing animals to move around, find mates and maintain gene flow between different populations,” says Yara de Melo Barros, executive director of the Onças do Iguaçu Project, one of the organizations involved in Tape’ỹ’s rescue and release. Iguaçu is part of the so-called Green Corridor, which crosses the Brazil-Argentina border and is home to about one-third of the fewer than 300 jaguars still surviving in the Atlantic Forest. It is an important habitat for the species, but highly fragmented and almost completely cut off from the rest of the biome, according to the most comprehensive assessment to date of connectivity across the jaguar’s range throughout the Americas, recently published in the journal Global Change Biology. Tape’ỹ being examined after his rescue…This article was originally…
items.t: Study maps jaguars across the Americas to help their populations rebound

items.title: Better data can help restore Himalayan ecosystems & prepare for climate risks (commentary)
items.summary: In less than seven weeks, two major flood events impacted Nepal’s Himalaya, where ecologically rich mountain landscapes are closely connected to the rivers, forests and floodplains. On the morning of Aug. 26, 2026, a catastrophic flood began with a rock and ice collapse on the northern flank of Langtang Lirung, within Langtang National Park. The park is one of country’s major Himalayan protected areas and provides habitat for species like Himalayan musk deer (Moschus leucogaster), Asiatic black bear (Ursus thibetanus), red panda (Ailurus fulgens) and clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa). Then, on Oct. 11, another destructive flood occurred in the Budhi Gandaki basin after a landslide blocked the river near Chumchet village in Gorkha District within the Manaslu Conservation Area that supports snow leopard (Panthera uncia), musk deer, blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur) and Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), along with more than 200 recorded Himalayan plant species. While the human cost of these disasters and the damage to physical infrastructure have been reported extensively, much less attention has gone to what they are doing to ecosystems and wildlife in the region. In the Himalaya, because of the extraordinary diversity and interconnectedness, any disturbance created in a high mountain valley can affect forests, wetlands and floodplains much further downstream. Some of the immediate effects are already visible after the recent events, but their ecological and longer-term consequences require systematic assessment. Research on earlier Himalayan disasters shows that major…

Abdul Goni Gazi fainted with fear during his first big cat encounter but now his mission is to help them coexist with people

items.title: Lucio Usobiaga wins 2026 ‘Nobel Prize of Gastronomy’ for protecting Mexico’s chinampas ecosystem
items.summary: Lucio Usobiaga of Mexico won the 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize for his project Arca Tierra, a network of farmers and the culinary community of Mexico that helps preserve Mexico City’s traditional chinampa agricultural system. The chinampas are an ancient, pre-Aztec series of agricultural canal islands, where small artificial plots of land were built in the wetlands of Xochimilco, in the southern valley of Mexico City. Traditional farmers known as chinamperos still practice this form of agriculture, growing flowers, maize, legumes, and several types of vegetables, Mongabay’s Aimee Gabay reported in 2024. The Basque Culinary World Prize, also referred to as the “Nobel Prize of Gastronomy,” was created in 2016 by the government of the Basque autonomous region in Spain and the Basque Culinary Center, and awards 100,000 euros (about $110,000) to a project chosen by the winner. Arca Tierra cultivates 6 hectares (about 15 acres) within the chinampas and works with 50 farming families across Xochimilco, Puebla, Hidalgo, and the state of Mexico. These farms supply around 60 restaurants in Mexico City with fresh produce.  According to Food & Wine magazine, the chinampa soil’s high organic matter from lake sediments also gives food grown there a special flavor. “I can tell, like from the first bite, when I’m eating a beet from the chinampas,” Usobiaga told Food & Wine.  Usobiaga told Mongabay by email that he wants people to know the chinampero farmers have been living in the chinampas for millennia, and that their important work has mostly gone unseen.  “Mexico City’s future is…
items.t: Lucio Usobiaga wins 2026 ‘Nobel Prize of Gastronomy’ for protecting Mexico’s chinampas ecosystem

items.title: Wildlife trafficking persists in West, Central Africa despite crackdowns: Report
items.summary: At his storefront in Lagos’s sprawling Lekki Craft Market, alongside handwoven raffia baskets and Ankara fabrics, an illegal wildlife trader, identified only as Mr. X, sells an array of carved ivory products. It’s from this shop that he established links with buyers across Asia, sending out large volumes of wildlife products sourced from the forests of Gabon, Cameroon, and the Central African Republic. In early 2022, Mr. X was arrested for unlawful possession of nearly 900 kilograms (nearly 2,000 pounds) of pangolin scales and 145 kg (320 lb) of elephant ivory. His operations ceased, and in May 2023, he was convicted and sentenced to two years in prison. But within months, Mr. X was free. Some 18 months later, investigators found that he was once again offering up pangolin scales for sale. Business had rebounded. Investigators found that Mr. X had likely spent only a few months in custody and reportedly paid several million naira, the equivalent of a few thousand U.S. dollars, in bribes through his lawyer during court proceedings. The saga of Mr. X is emblematic of the ongoing corruption and persistence of West and Central Africa’s illegal wildlife trade that’s pushing many species to the brink, despite better enforcement in recent years, according to a new report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), an international NGO that digs into environmental crimes across the world. Criminal networks, investigators found, have continued to evolve and evade efforts to clamp down on the flow of products derived from imperiled wildlife.…This article was originally…
items.t: Wildlife trafficking persists in West, Central Africa despite crackdowns: Report

items.title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares
items.summary:
Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here

For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale.

As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight.

Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

items.title: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous Awá people in Brazil exposes vulnerability
items.summary: On Nov. 16, a group of roughly 20 Indigenous Awá people living in voluntary isolation approached an Indigenous Guajajara village, in Brazil’s northeastern Maranhão state. The rare encounter has mobilized Indigenous peoples and activists concerned about the safety of the Awá, considered the most threatened group on the planet. The motivation for the unusual interaction is unclear, but Guajajara leaders “expressed concern about the physical condition of some members of the group, especially children and older people, who appeared to be very thin,” according to accounts and images posted on social media by Indigenous organizations. The Guajajara reportedly offered the Awá food and other objects; the Awá remained there briefly before returning to the forest. Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, told Mongabay by email that technical teams are monitoring the situation and that it had activated a contingency plan to “ensure that the relevant agencies are prepared to respond appropriately to any developments in the situation, especially regarding the ethno-environmental protection, health and safety of the Indigenous people involved.” Funai added that the peoples’ right to self-determination would continue to be respected. Unlike other isolated peoples who make frequent contact, this is the first time in decades that the Awá of the Arariboia Indigenous Territory “have appeared in this way and made such close contact with other people,” Sarah Shenker, director and senior researcher at the Indigenous rights organization Survival International Brazil, told Mongabay by phone.…
items.t: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous Awá people in Brazil exposes vulnerability

items.title: Jason Clay, who persuaded big business to help save nature, has died at 75
items.summary: In 1988 Jason Clay attended a Grateful Dead concert at Madison Square Garden and met a man who wanted to help save tropical rainforests. Clay, an anthropologist who had worked with Indigenous communities, asked what he did for a living. “I make ice cream,” the man replied. It was Ben Cohen of Ben & Jerry’s. Clay suggested developing a flavor using nuts gathered from tropical forests. He thought higher payments for forest products might give people a reason to keep the trees standing. Within a year, Rainforest Crunch was on supermarket shelves. Clay set up a trading company and went on to work with more than 50 businesses on some 200 products, generating roughly $100 million in retail sales. At one point, he said, his operation was buying around a fifth of the world’s Brazil nuts. It paid gatherers two or three times the going rate, and other buyers raised their prices to compete. The people gathering the nuts weren’t generally the ones clearing the forests. Ranchers and loggers had little reason to change what they were doing, and Clay eventually called Rainforest Crunch a failure. “We were attacking the wrong driver,” he explained in a 2010 TED talk. He should have been working on beef, lumber and soy. Clay, who died on November 16th aged 75, spent more than three decades at the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), where he worked to change how major companies bought agricultural commodities linked to deforestation and other environmental problems. Born in 1951,…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Jason Clay, who persuaded big business to help save nature, has died at 75

items.title: In Zimbabwe, trusted local guardians help communities coexist with lions
items.summary: Conservation biologist and founder of the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action, Moreangels Mbizah joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail her work helping reduce human-wildlife conflict between African lions and communities in Zimbabwe. The group began working only six years ago in two wards of Nyaminyami rural district, and since then has recorded a 98% reduction in conflict incidents there. Across the districts of Mbire and Binga, conflict has decreased by 53%. To accomplish this, WCA has pioneered a “community guardian” model. Known as “Batabilili,” these guardians are trained by the organization and implement a range of mitigation measures, including helping farmers secure livestock in above-ground kraals, monitoring lion movement, and conducting community meetings. “They are trusted because they come from these communities, and they are their children, their brothers and sisters,” Mbizah says. “They are part of the community fabric, so that makes it really important in terms of the buy-in and the ideas and the decisions that are being made when it comes to lion conservation.” She says this has also helped reduce retaliatory killings of lions for preying on livestock, because community members’ concerns are directly addressed by a trusted member. “There’s no one that is supporting them when they incur these losses. No one comes to see and to support, to provide … emotional or psychological support when a conflict incident happen[s]. So we wanted to change that,” Mbizah says. “They always felt that [the] wildlife authority, they care about wildlife and they…
items.t: In Zimbabwe, trusted local guardians help communities coexist with lions

items.title: Prince William’s presents Earthshot Prize winners with $1.3M each in Mumbai
items.summary: MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William presented five Earthshot Prize winners with 1 million pounds ($1.3 million) each on Tuesday, recognizing their efforts to tackle the world’s climate challenges. The annual ceremony, held this year in Mumbai, marked the centerpiece of William and Princess Catherine’s three-day visit to India. The Earthshot Prize winners were selected from 15 finalists for their work in areas ranging from clean transport and renewable energy to forest conservation and marine protection. Four were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its electric transport initiatives; PFAS-Free France, for its campaign to ban toxic “forever chemicals”; Niue Ocean Wide Trust, for protecting marine ecosystems; and Ørsted, for advancing offshore wind energy. The fifth recipient was the country of Bhutan for its work in conserving Himalayan forests. William, the Prince of Wales, established the prize through his Royal Foundation in 2020 to encourage inventors and entrepreneurs to develop technologies to combat global warming and mitigate its effects. The ceremony at Mumbai’s Jio World Convention Centre brought together Bollywood celebrities, innovators, entrepreneurs and environmental advocates. William and the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, began their visit Monday. The couple have played street cricket in Mumbai, ridden in an electric rickshaw and met leading figures from India’s cricket, fashion and film industries. They are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday. The trip marks a significant step in Kate’s return to overseas royal…
items.t: Prince William’s presents Earthshot Prize winners with $1.3M each in Mumbai

items.title: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad
items.summary: The scimitar-horned oryx, an antelope with a majestic set of sword-like horns, had disappeared from Chad by the late 1980s and was declared extinct in the wild globally in 2000. But now, thanks to a reintroduction program led by the NGO Sahara Conservation, its conservation status has improved to “endangered.” The oryx population in Ouadi Rimé–Ouadi Achim Wildlife Reserve, Chad’s largest protected area, has grown from 25 individuals in 2016 to 700 today. That makes it the largest herd in the world. However, the species continues to face challenges, including climate change impacts such as prolonged droughts and shifting conditions, as well as competition from livestock for grazing lands.This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad

items.title: You’ve Probably Seen This Famous Meme Dog, But Here’s The Heartwarming Story Behind Her
items.summary:
If you’ve spent enough time scrolling through social media, there’s a good chance you’ve seen this smiling little Jack Russell Terrier before. Her expressive face has appeared in countless memes, funny videos, and photos, often accompanied by music and some rather unusual captions.

Many people know her as Aifolou or Wenomechainsama, but her real name was Maya. And behind those familiar images was a Jack Russell Terrier from Ukraine whose owner, photographer Iryna Kalamurza , never expected her beloved pet to become an internet celebrity.

Iryna recently shared Maya’s story with us at Bored Panda , revealing how their nearly 16 years together led to a photography project that would eventually make the little dog famous worldwide. Scroll down to read the full story and see how Maya’s studio photos slowly morphed into online memes and countless examples of fan art.

More info: aifolou.com | Instagram | kalamurza.com 

Maya was just a puppy when Iryna met her at a breeder’s home near Kyiv, Ukraine, in the summer of 2010 

maya_dog_jrt 

Their story began in the summer of 2010, when Iryna visited a dog breeder near Kyiv, Ukraine. She had always dreamed of owning a Jack Russell Terrier, and although the breeder kept recommending a different puppy, she immediately felt drawn to Maya. “I just felt that she was my dog,” Iryna recalled.

Although the breeder recommended another puppy, Iryna couldn’t take her eyes off Maya and immediately knew she was the one 

maya_dog_jrt 

The two became inseparable, spending nearly 16 years together and traveling to different countries…
items.t: Meet Maya, The Internet-Famous Dog Whose Photos Became Countless Memes Around The World

items.title: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting
items.summary:
Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

items.t: Band of baby sea turtles swims out to sea after historic California nesting

items.title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
items.summary:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

  • Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.

Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

Continue reading...
items.t: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
items.t: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
items.summary:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

Continue reading...
items.t: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests

items.title: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell
items.summary:
Brigg, Lincolnshire: As I turn to the autumn jobs, loading crops and checking our machinery, I have to feel that next year will be better

The days are suddenly short, and the mornings have begun to turn much colder, but – strange as it may seem – I’m feeling optimistic. This happens every year around now – I look around and see well-established winter crops full of potential, hedges and edges full of food for the wildlife, and, for now, some money back in the bank, having sold some of the harvest.

The changing colours help – not only the trees but also the yellow and the browns of the soil changing back to green. Farmers have to be the ultimate gamblers, planting a crop with no idea what price we will achieve or what yield will come. We plant and hope.

Continue reading...
items.t: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

items.t: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
items.t: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

items.title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards | Letters
items.summary:
Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny

Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).

I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

items.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
items.summary:
Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes.

Continue reading...
items.t: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
